body.statement: For every \(d\in\mathcal D_L\cap(0,1)^p\), the population Gram matrix is positive definite and \[\Phi_k(d)=\sum_{T\in\mathcal I_k}\prod_{i\in T}r(d_i)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}e_j(r(d_1),\ldots,r(d_p)).\] If any coordinate of \(d\) equals zero or one, then \(\Sigma_k(d)\) is singular and \(\Phi_k(d)=+\infty\). The interior identity is obtained by the triangular change from the fixed monomials to product-orthonormal features and is the Bernoulli specialization of the downward-closed product-design identity of Schwabe and Wong.
body.proof_tex:
Put \(m_i=\mathbb E_d[X_{ai}]=2d_i-1\) and \(v_i=1-m_i^2=4d_i(1-d_i)\). First suppose that \(d\in(0,1)^p\), so every \(v_i>0\). For \(T\in\mathcal I_k\), define
\[
 \psi_T(X_a)=\prod_{i\in T}\frac{X_{ai}-m_i}{\sqrt{v_i}}.
\]
By product randomization, factors belonging to different coordinates are independent. Each standardized factor has mean zero and second moment one. Hence, for \(T,U\in\mathcal I_k\),
\[
 \mathbb E_d[\psi_T\psi_U]=\mathbf 1\{T=U\}.
\]
Indeed, when \(T\ne U\), a coordinate in \(T\triangle U\) occurs to the first power and contributes a zero factor to the product expectation. Expanding each centered product gives
\[
 \psi_T
 =\sum_{S\subseteq T}
 \frac{\prod_{i\in T\setminus S}(-m_i)}{\prod_{i\in T}\sqrt{v_i}}\,\phi_S.
\]
All sets \(S\subseteq T\) remain in \(\mathcal I_k\), because that family is downward closed. Thus \(\psi=A\phi\), where
\[
 A_{T,S}=\mathbf 1\{S\subseteq T\}
 \frac{\prod_{i\in T\setminus S}(-m_i)}{\prod_{i\in T}\sqrt{v_i}}.
\]
In any ordering compatible with inclusion, \(A\) is triangular and its diagonal entry in row \(T\) is \(\prod_{i\in T}v_i^{-1/2}>0\). Consequently \(A\) is invertible. Orthonormality and the definition of \(\Sigma_k(d)\) yield
\[
 A\Sigma_k(d)A^{\mathsf T}=I_q,
 \qquad
 \Sigma_k(d)^{-1}=A^{\mathsf T}A.
\]
This proves positive definiteness and also gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Phi_k(d)
 &=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\mathsf T}A)
 =\sum_{T\in\mathcal I_k}\sum_{S\subseteq T}A_{T,S}^2\\
 &=\sum_{T\in\mathcal I_k}
 \frac{\prod_{i\in T}(1+m_i^2)}{\prod_{i\in T}(1-m_i^2)}
 =\sum_{T\in\mathcal I_k}\prod_{i\in T}r(d_i).
\end{aligned}
\]
The penultimate equality follows by factoring the sum over \(S\subseteq T\), and the last follows from
\[
 \frac{1+m_i^2}{1-m_i^2}
 =\frac{d_i^2+(1-d_i)^2}{2d_i(1-d_i)}
 =\frac1{2d_i(1-d_i)}-1=r(d_i).
\]
Grouping subsets by cardinality is precisely the elementary-symmetric representation
\[
 \Phi_k(d)=\sum_{j=0}^k e_j(r(d_1),\ldots,r(d_p)).
\]
If \(d_i=0\), then \(X_{ai}=-1\) almost surely, so the singleton column \(\phi_{\{i\}}\) equals minus the intercept column. If \(d_i=1\), it equals the intercept column. Since \(k\ge1\), both columns are retained; hence \(\Sigma_k(d)\) is singular and the extended-real definition gives \(\Phi_k(d)=+\infty\).

For the announced classical attribution, the marginal information matrix for \((1,X_i)\) is
\[
 M_i=\begin{pmatrix}1&m_i\\m_i&1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{tr}(M_i^{-1})-1
 =\frac{1+m_i^2}{1-m_i^2}=r(d_i).
\]
Substitution into the cited downward-closed product-design identity gives exactly the same displayed formula.

Finally, the requested smallest exact check succeeds. For \(p=3\), \(k=2\), at \(d=(1/3,1/3,1/3)\), all three factors equal \(5/4\), and therefore
\[
 \Phi_2(d)=1+3\frac54+3\left(\frac54\right)^2=\frac{151}{16}.
\]
At \(d=(1/4,1/3,5/12)\), the factors are \(5/3,5/4,37/35\), so
\[
 \Phi_2(d)=1+\frac{1669}{420}+\frac{217}{42}=\frac{4259}{420}.
\]
Thus the early-kill calculation agrees with the identity.
body.justification: This representation removes the higher-order characteristic-polynomial obstruction and exposes separable curvature.
body.gap: SchwabeWong1999 contains the general identity, while ShyamalZhangUhler2025 does not specialize it to solve the shared-supply all-order problem.
body.consumer: The identity turns the interaction-design problem into an explicit scalar symmetric-polynomial optimization usable by the dosage theorem.
